subject: geography
title: The Nile and the Sahara
welcome_lead: Sand, sun and water! Explore the world's longest river and largest hot desert side by side.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on the Nile river and the Sahara desert.
final_note: Excellent! You now know two of Africa's most famous landscapes.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Nile flows north from Lake Victoria through 11 countries to the Mediterranean. Egypt's ancient civilisation grew along its fertile banks.
The Sahara covers about 9 million km² — bigger than the USA! It includes dunes, rocky plateaus and salt flats. Daytime temperatures can top 45°C.
People like the Tuareg have lived in the Sahara for centuries, trading along old caravan routes. They cluster around oases.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model?
options: Birth rates rise rapidly because people want larger families.
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
Death rates fall rapidly (due to better food, sanitation and medicine) while birth rates remain high, causing rapid population growth.
Mitigation is done by HICs and adaptation is done by LICs.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between glacial abrasion and plucking?
options: Abrasion is when wind erodes the glacier and plucking is when rain does.
Abrasion: rock embedded in the glacier base scrapes the bedrock smooth, creating striations. Plucking: meltwater refreezes onto bedrock, then movement rips chunks of rock away.
Mitigation is done by HICs and adaptation is done by LICs.
Abrasion and plucking are different words for the same process.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation to climate change?
options: Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
Mitigation and adaptation mean the same thing — both are about stopping climate change.
Mitigation is done by HICs and adaptation is done by LICs.
Mitigation reduces the causes (cutting greenhouse gas emissions); adaptation reduces the impacts (e.g. building sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning systems).
